# What Predicts Correctness in Text-to-SQL? A Selective-Prediction Study

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#selective-prediction)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06799v1) · arXiv:2607.06799v1, 7 July 2026

**Reading coverage:** All 11 PDF pages: Sections 1-7, Appendices A-B, Tables 1-7 and both figures. Figures 1-2 visually inspected.

## Research question

Estimate whether a generated query should be answered or withheld, using reference-execution correctness as the target.

## Method

Compares sampled agreement, probabilities, schema relevance, executability, frozen judges and trained verifiers. Cross-fit logistic calibration combines provider scores; separate calibration/test halves select abstention thresholds.

## Evaluation

Uses an 800-question, eight-database BIRD convenience slice and 490 multi-table Spider questions. Transfer uses leave-one-database-out evaluation; bootstrap intervals and an additional conservative certificate are reported.

## What the results support

The two-provider ensemble reports AUROC 0.822 and ECE 0.031 on the BIRD slice. Trained verifiers perform better within known schemas than on held-out databases; strong judges outperform sampled agreement in the tested configurations.

## Limits and qualifications

These are dataset/model-specific comparisons, not a universal consistency ceiling. The abstract places statistical signals around 0.61-0.68, but Table 1 lists schema relevance 0.553 and executability 0.500. Figure 1 does not support its caption's claim that the frozen judge leads on every database.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Separates empirical risk-coverage from certified bounds and candidate correctness from request answerability.
